questions.question: How many bones comprise the complete adult human skeletal system?
questions.explanation: The adult human skeleton has 206 bones (80 axial + 126 appendicular), down from ~270 at birth due to bone fusion.

questions.question: How many bones are in the Axial Skeleton of an adult human?
questions.explanation: The axial skeleton consists of 80 bones: skull (28), hyoid (1), vertebral column (26), ribs (24), and sternum (1).

questions.question: What is the fundamental microscopic structural unit of compact bone?
questions.explanation: An osteon consists of concentric lamellae of bone matrix surrounding a central Haversian canal containing blood vessels and nerves.

questions.question: Which mature bone cells reside in small spaces called lacunae and maintain mineral homeostasis in bone tissue?
questions.explanation: Osteocytes are mature bone cells derived from osteoblasts, connected via canaliculi to monitor mechanical strain and mineral balance.

questions.question: Which multinucleated giant cells secrete acid and enzymes to resorb and break down bone matrix during remodeling?
questions.explanation: Osteoclasts are macrophage-lineage bone-resorbing cells that demineralize matrix to release calcium into blood.

questions.question: Which type of cartilage is the most abundant in the human body, covering articular ends of long bones and forming costal cartilages?
questions.explanation: Hyaline cartilage provides a glassy, smooth, low-friction surface at synovial joints, the respiratory tract, and costal margins.

questions.question: Which tough, shock-absorbing cartilage forms the intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis?
questions.explanation: Fibrocartilage has dense parallel bundles of Type I collagen, resisting heavy compression in intervertebral discs and menisci.

questions.question: What type of joint allows the widest range of multiaxial movement, such as the shoulder and hip joints?
questions.explanation: Ball-and-socket joints permit universal triaxial movement: flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction, and rotation.

questions.question: Which type of joint permits movement primarily in a single uniaxial plane, like a door hinge (e.g., elbow and knee joints)?
questions.explanation: Hinge joints restrict movement to one plane (flexion and extension), exemplified by the humeroulnar joint at the elbow.

questions.question: What is the tough, fibrous connective tissue that connects muscle to bone?
questions.explanation: Tendons connect muscle bellies to bones, transmitting contractile forces to move skeletal levers.

questions.question: What connective tissue bands connect bone to bone, stabilizing joints and limiting excess motion?
questions.explanation: Ligaments are strong fibrous bands linking bones together at joints, preventing dislocation.

questions.question: What is the functional contractile unit of a skeletal muscle fiber, extending from one Z-line to the next Z-line?
questions.explanation: The sarcomere is the repeating contractile unit between adjacent Z-discs, containing overlapping thin and thick myofilaments.

questions.question: Which protein forms the thick myofilaments with globular heads capable of binding actin and hydrolyzing ATP?
questions.explanation: Thick filaments consist of myosin molecules with elongated tails and mobile globular heads possessing ATPase activity.

questions.question: Which regulatory protein blocks the myosin-binding sites on actin thin filaments when a skeletal muscle is at rest?
questions.explanation: In relaxed muscle, filamentous tropomyosin lies along the actin groove, physically obstructing myosin heads from binding.

questions.question: During muscle contraction, to which regulatory protein do Calcium ions ($Ca^{2+}$) bind, causing a conformational shift that exposes myosin-binding sites on actin?
questions.explanation: $Ca^{2+}$ binds to Troponin C, pulling tropomyosin away from actin active sites to allow cross-bridge formation.

questions.question: According to the Sliding Filament Theory of muscle contraction, what happens to the sarcomere during active contraction?

options.A: Thin actin filaments slide over thick myosin filaments toward the M-line; the H-zone and I-band narrow while the A-band length remains constant
options.B: Both actin and myosin filaments physically shrink in length
options.C: The A-band length triples while Z-lines push apart
options.D: Myosin filaments detach and dissolve into sarcoplasm

questions.explanation: Myofilaments do not shorten; actin slides inward over myosin, narrowing the I-band and H-zone while the A-band remains unchanged.

questions.question: Where are Calcium ions ($Ca^{2+}$) sequestered and stored inside a relaxed muscle fiber before release into the sarcoplasm?
questions.explanation: The sarcoplasmic reticulum stores high concentrations of $Ca^{2+}$ via active SERCA pumps, releasing them upon membrane depolarization.

questions.question: What is the primary role of the Transverse Tubule (T-tubule) system in muscle fibers?

options.A: Conducting electrical action potentials from the sarcolemma deep into the interior of the muscle fiber to trigger calcium release

questions.explanation: T-tubules are invaginations of the sarcolemma that propagate action potentials deep into the cell to synchronize calcium release from the SR.

questions.question: What causes 'Rigor Mortis' (stiffness of death) several hours after clinical death?

options.A: Complete depletion of cellular ATP prevents myosin heads from detaching from actin binding sites, locking cross-bridges in place
options.B: Rapid synthesis of excess bone matrix around joints
options.C: Enzymatic destruction of all muscle cell membranes

questions.explanation: Detachment of myosin heads requires fresh ATP binding. When ATP stores hit zero post-mortem, cross-bridges remain rigidly locked.

questions.question: What is 'All-or-None Principle' in skeletal muscle physiology?

options.A: An individual muscle fiber contracts completely or not at all in response to a threshold stimulus
options.B: All muscles in the human body contract simultaneously
options.C: A bone breaks completely or suffers zero damage
options.D: All calcium ions must be converted into bone crystals

questions.explanation: A single muscle fiber generates maximal tension for given physiological conditions once the action potential threshold is reached.

questions.question: How do skeletal muscles grade the total force of contraction if individual fibers follow the all-or-none rule?

options.A: Motor Unit Recruitment (varying the number of active motor units and firing frequency)
options.C: By changing the length of myosin myofilaments
options.D: By altering the chemical structure of hemoglobin

questions.explanation: Graded muscle tension is produced by recruiting more motor units (spatial summation) and increasing stimulation frequency (temporal wave summation).

questions.question: What high-energy phosphate molecule stored in skeletal muscle rapidly donates a phosphate group to ADP to replenish ATP during the first few seconds of intense exercise?
questions.explanation: Creatine phosphate donates a high-energy phosphate to ADP via creatine kinase, regenerating ATP rapidly during initial explosive contraction.

questions.question: What metabolic byproduct accumulates in muscle fibers during prolonged vigorous anaerobic exertion, contributing to muscle fatigue and acidosis?
questions.explanation: Anaerobic glycolysis reduces pyruvate to lactate, generating $H^+$ ions that lower sarcoplasmic pH and inhibit contractile enzymes.

questions.question: Which skeletal condition is characterized by progressive loss of bone mineral density, weakening microarchitecture, and increased fracture risk, common in postmenopausal women?
questions.explanation: Osteoporosis results when bone resorption by osteoclasts outpaces bone formation by osteoblasts, exacerbated by postmenopausal estrogen decline.

questions.question: What nutritional deficiency in children causes 'Rickets', characterized by soft, weak bones and bowed legs?
questions.explanation: Vitamin D is required for intestinal calcium absorption; deficiency impairs bone mineralization, leading to rickets in children.

questions.question: Which inflammatory joint disease is caused by the deposition of monosodium urate crystals in synovial joints (most commonly the big toe)?
questions.explanation: Hyperuricemia leads to needle-like urate crystal precipitation in joints, triggering severe inflammation known as gout.

questions.question: What type of joint disorder is characterized by wear-and-tear degeneration of articular cartilage and formation of bone spurs (osteophytes)?
questions.explanation: Osteoarthritis is a chronic degenerative joint disease involving progressive mechanical erosion of articular cartilage.

questions.question: What is the primary autoimmune feature of Rheumatoid Arthritis?

options.A: The immune system attacks the synovial membrane, causing chronic proliferative synovitis (pannus formation) and joint destruction
options.B: Bacterial infection inside bone marrow cavities

questions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition where antibodies target synovial membranes, leading to pannus tissue and joint deformity.

questions.question: Which bone of the human forearm lies lateral in the anatomical position and rotates around the ulna during supination/pronation?
questions.explanation: The radius is on the lateral (thumb) side of the forearm, pivoting around the medial ulna at the radioulnar joints.

questions.question: Which long bone is the longest, heaviest, and strongest in the human body?
questions.explanation: The femur is the longest, heaviest, and strongest human bone, supporting body weight during bipedal standing and locomotion.

questions.question: What is a 'Herniated Disc' (slipped disc)?

options.A: Rupture of the outer fibrous ring (annulus fibrosus) allowing the inner gel-like nucleus pulposus to protrude and compress spinal nerves
options.D: Sprain of the knee cruciate ligament

questions.explanation: Herniation occurs when the gelatinous nucleus pulposus bulges through a torn annulus fibrosus, pinching adjacent spinal nerve roots.

questions.question: What is the difference between a 'Sprain' and a 'Strain' in sports medicine?

options.A: A sprain is an injury to a ligament, while a strain is an injury to a muscle or tendon
options.B: A sprain involves fractured bone, while a strain is joint inflammation
options.C: A sprain occurs only in the brain, while a strain occurs in the heart
options.D: There is no medical distinction between the two

questions.explanation: Sprains involve stretched or torn ligaments (joint stabilizers); strains involve overstretched or torn muscle fibers or tendons.

questions.question: Which type of muscle tissue is striated, branched, uninucleated, and joined by intercalated discs with gap junctions?
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle fibers are branched and connected by intercalated discs containing gap junctions that coordinate electrical syncytium contraction.

questions.question: Which muscle tissue is non-striated, involuntary, spindle-shaped, and lines hollow visceral organs (intestines, blood vessels)?
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle lacks microscopic sarcomeric striations, contracting involuntarily in digestive, vascular, and reproductive walls.

questions.question: In neuromuscular transmission, which neurotransmitter is released from the presynaptic motor neuron terminal into the synaptic cleft?
questions.explanation: ACh is released from motor axon terminals, binding to nicotinic receptors on the muscle endplate to trigger depolarization.
